The plan envisions reducing Volkswagen's work force by 50,000, phasing out four factories in Germany to eliminate expensive excess production capacity, and slimming the company's roughly 150 different models to half that.

articles.title: Volkswagen CEO faces angry workers in push for radical cuts
articles.summary: STORY: :: Berlin, Germany / August 25, 2026 :: Rachel More, Automotive Correspondent :: What happened at Volkswagen's meeting in Wolfsburg? "So today in Wolfsburg was the first chance for Volkswagen workers to grill the CEO Oliver Bluma on his plans to restructure the company. He is basically touring the Volkswagen plants in Germany this week to try and explain to workers why these cuts are necessary. We're talking about 50,000 job cuts that he says would be necessary to make Volkswagen competitive and the possible closure of certain factories, some of which he will be visiting this week. And we had more than 10,000 workers gathered in Wolfsburg today, which is not slated for possible closure, but is very symbolic as Volkswagen's headquarters. And... It was quite a tense atmosphere, what we're hearing from participants at the meeting." :: What did labor leaders say on Tuesday? "The head of Volkswagen's Works Council, Daniella Cavallo, said that there had been damage to their confidence in Bluma. They've been very upset on the Labor side that a lot of these proposed cuts have appeared first in media. They want more open communication with the workforce, but she said it wasn't irreparable and... We know that the Labor side and the state of Lower Saxony are going into these talks on further restructuring talks now with their own proposals, saying that they want to work with management. They agree that the situation is not good for Volkswagen. There are challenges from Chinese competition, billions of euros in annual tariff costs, generally weak demand in Europe. Everyone is agreed on that. But the Labor side did reiterate today its opposition to mandatory redundancies and plant closures, and said that if management doesn't move away from its course of only looking for cuts, that there will be quite a battle ahead."

articles.title: Volkswagen workers criticize board's communication
articles.summary: STORY: Volkswagen employees aren't happy with management. :: 'disastrous external communication' Here's why they accused the carmaker's board of "disastrous external communication." :: largest-ever restructuring Volkswagen is undergoing what is seen to be its largest-ever restructuring. :: 50,000 job cuts It could possibly range from a further 50,000 job cuts to the carve-out of some divisions. The criticism over communications was seen by Reuters in an internal VW works council article as VW management looks at further cost cuts :: unsettled and frightened An online survey by the works council found employees and their families were - quote - "unsettled and frightened" by the board's public communications. Employees also raised concerns about job security, severance programs and the future of early-retirment. :: Zwickau :: Neckarsulm :: Hanover :: Osnabrueck :: Emden. They were also worried about the future of major VW plants in at least five locations, Including Zwickau, Neckarsulm, Hanover, Osnabrueck and Emden. CEO Oliver Blume said in an internal memo Friday four of those plants weren't expected to reach competitive capacity utilization in the 2030s. :: 'no decision yet' But he said there was no decision yet on specific plant closures. Blume has also rejected accusations of withholding information. He said in July, - quote - "We continuously keep our colleagues and employee representatives informed about the status of the plans." Blume will address employees at an extraordinary meeting in Wolfsburg on Tuesday.
